vignette:
He is 34, a South Eastern Asian man who has spent most of his adult life learning how to sit with other people's grief. As a chaplain, he moves quietly through hospital corridors, family waiting rooms, and small chapel spaces, speaking in a steady voice that people seem to trust. Before the robbery, he describes himself as someone who could enter almost any room and make it feel calmer. He had already known loss by then; his wife died several years earlier, and he often says that becoming widowed deepened his ministry. He believed suffering could be carried, if not removed, by being present with it.

The mugging happens late one evening after he leaves the hospital. He has stayed past his shift with a family whose father is dying, and by the time he walks to his car the parking lot is mostly empty. He notices footsteps behind him but tells himself not to be dramatic. When the man comes up fast and grabs him, he freezes for a split second, confused more than afraid. Then he sees the weapon. He remembers the shine of it under the parking lot light and the smell of stale smoke on the man's clothes. The robber shoves him against the side of his car, demands his wallet and phone, and keeps shouting even after he hands them over. He is sure, in those few moments, that he is about to die. He thinks strangely of his wife, not as a memory but as a fact-he is going to see her. When the man strikes him and runs, he slides to the ground and stays there, unable to understand that the attack is over.

In the days afterward, he tells almost no one how frightened he was. He reports the robbery, replaces his cards, answers practical questions. Colleagues notice the bruise on his face and his stiffness, and he minimizes it. He says he was "just unlucky." What unsettles him is not only what happened but how completely helpless he felt. He starts replaying the attack at odd times: in the shower, while blessing a meal, while listening to a family describe a sudden death. The memory does not come to him as a narrative. It arrives as flashes-the metal, the shouting, the pressure of the car against his back. His body reacts before his mind catches up. His chest tightens, his hands go cold, and he scans for exits without meaning to.

Sleep changes first. He begins waking at 2 or 3 in the morning, heart racing, already alert. Sometimes he has dreams in which he is back in the parking lot, unable to speak. Other nights the dream shifts and it is his wife being threatened while he stands by uselessly. He stops parking in the employee lot where the robbery occurred and starts taking rides when he can, even if it means waiting an extra hour after work. If he has to walk alone anywhere after dark, he grips his keys between his fingers and feels ashamed of how frightened he is.

At work, the change is subtle but significant. He still shows up, still prays with patients, still knows the right words. But he no longer lingers in rooms. He positions himself near doors. If a visitor raises his voice, even in grief, he feels a jolt of panic and has to concentrate to remain still. He used to volunteer for overnight on-call shifts because he felt called to be available in moments of crisis. Now he trades them away. He tells himself it is because of poor sleep, but underneath that is the dread of crossing dark parking lots and empty hallways. He feels hypocritical when he speaks to others about courage or peace. He hears himself saying, "You are safe here," while his own mind keeps insisting that nowhere is safe.

Outside work, his world narrows. Since his wife died, he had built a careful life of routines-morning tea, calls with his sister, weekly dinners with a small circle from his faith community. After the robbery, he begins canceling plans. Restaurants with glass fronts make him uneasy because he wants to see everyone entering. He chooses corners in coffee shops where no one can approach from behind. At home he checks the lock three or four times before bed. Small sounds-a motorcycle backfiring, footsteps on the stairs outside his apartment, a stranger speaking too loudly-send a spike of fear through him that feels disproportionate and humiliating. He is especially distressed by his irritability. He snaps at a volunteer for coming up behind him in the chapel sacristy, then feels immediate remorse when he sees the young man's startled face.

He talks often about the spiritual meaning he once made of suffering and how inaccessible that meaning feels now. He has not lost his faith, but it no longer offers the same shelter. He prays and finds himself distracted by images of the weapon. During memorial services, when families speak about sudden violence or unfairness, he feels both pierced and estranged. Part of him is still in that parking lot, waiting for the next blow. Another part judges him for not being stronger, especially as someone others come to for comfort.

In session, he is composed until he describes the moment he thought he would die. Then his voice thins and his eyes move toward the door. He says he knows, logically, that the robbery lasted only minutes. His body does not seem to know that. Months later, he still lives as if danger is just behind him, close enough to smell.
